title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database executed a schema migration command against live data instead of a test environment. The agent was given direct credentials to production and autonomy to resolve database issues without human review of its commands. The command itself was not inherently destructive, but pointed to the wrong target because production and test credentials were not properly separated.

The failure was deployment without adequate guardrails. A human would have caught this before execution if the system required approval for commands affecting production, or if database access had been restricted to non-production environments only. The agent itself detected and reported the error after the tables were already emptied, showing that detection was possible but came too late.

It is not established whether similar incidents have occurred with this system, whether the developer had received training in safe practices, or what specific safeguards were recommended but not implemented.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access permissions. The developer instructed the agent to analyze a project repository and resolve schema issues autonomously. However, a Prisma migration command intended for a disposable test database was instead directed at the production database URL. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all tables in the production database within approximately ten minutes, resulting in complete data loss.

The incident occurred because the command syntax itself was not inherently destructive, making it difficult to flag as dangerous. The risk stemmed entirely from the database credentials being unscoped and pointing to the wrong target. The agent detected the error and reported it to the developer before the damage was discovered through normal monitoring. The incident could have been prevented through guardrail controls that validate command targets against policy before execution, or by restricting the agent's database access to non-production environments only.
